title: Transient ischemic attack (transient deficit, normal CT): statin for secondary prevention
vignette: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to right upper extremity weakness. Thirty minutes ago, the patient was at his office when he developed difficulty holding a pen. His grip in the right hand was weak and he could not lift his right arm. He tried calling his coworker but could not speak. The patient has never had similar symptoms before. He had no loss of consciousness, weakness of other extremities, vision abnormality, or headache. The symptoms resolved spontaneously by the time paramedics arrived. Medical history is significant for hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history. The patient is a defense attorney and recently took on a high-profile case. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 140/84 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min and regular, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination shows no extremity weakness or sensory loss. There is a left carotid bruit; the remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Noncontrast CT scan of the head is normal. Which of the following pharmacotherapies is most appropriate in management of this patient?

clues.note: An acute focal neurologic deficit (unilateral arm weakness) localized to one vascular territory suggests cerebral ischemia.
Transient aphasia points to left-hemisphere (dominant) ischemia - consistent with the left carotid lesion.
Complete spontaneous resolution of focal deficits without infarction is characteristic of a TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK (TIA).
A carotid bruit indicates atherosclerotic carotid disease - a likely source of atheroembolism/low flow causing the TIA and a target for risk reduction.

clues.text: Noncontrast CT scan of the head is normal
clues.note: No infarction or hemorrhage on CT with resolved symptoms confirms a TIA (tissue infarction did not occur).

whatMatters: Transient focal deficits (arm weakness, aphasia) that RESOLVED, with a carotid bruit and a NORMAL CT = a TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK. Secondary stroke prevention includes antiplatelet therapy and a STATIN (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) to reduce atherosclerotic plaque. Answer C.
strategy: Recognize the TIA (deficit resolved, CT normal) and choose secondary prevention: antiplatelet + STATIN (and risk-factor control - BP, smoking). Reject tPA (thrombolysis is for an ACUTE disabling infarct with persistent deficits - not a resolved TIA, where it adds bleeding risk with no benefit), CNS immunomodulator (multiple sclerosis), GABA-A modulator/benzodiazepine (seizures - which give positive symptoms/postictal confusion), and SSRI (depression/anxiety).

eliminations.label: CNS immunomodulator - multiple sclerosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: disease-modifying therapy for MS (e.g., ocrelizumab) or glucocorticoids. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: MS causes relapsing-remitting deficits in young patients (often women) evolving over days, not a sudden vascular TIA in a 62-year-old with a carotid bruit. ✅ Correct if: demyelinating disease (MS).

eliminations.label: GABA-A modulator - seizure, not TIA
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a benzodiazepine for acute seizure termination. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: seizures usually cause POSITIVE symptoms (rhythmic movements) preceded by stereotyped activity and postictal confusion, whereas TIAs cause NEGATIVE deficits (loss of function); CT and history fit TIA. ✅ Correct if: acute seizure.

eliminations.label: SSRI - depression/anxiety
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an antidepressant/anxiolytic. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the stressful case is a red herring; the presentation is a focal vascular event, not a psychiatric one. ✅ Correct if: major depression or anxiety disorder.

eliminations.label: tPA - not for a resolved TIA
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: thrombolysis (alteplase) for acute ischemic stroke with persistent, potentially disabling deficits. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this patient's deficits RESOLVED (a TIA, no infarct on CT), so tPA offers no benefit and only bleeding risk. ✅ Correct if: acute disabling stroke within the thrombolysis window with an ongoing deficit.

reasoning: Sudden focal deficits (arm weakness, aphasia) that fully resolved = transient ischemic attack
A carotid bruit and normal CT support atheroembolic/low-flow TIA without infarction
TIA management is secondary prevention: antiplatelet + statin + risk-factor control
mechanism: A TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK (TIA) is a transient episode of FOCAL neurologic dysfunction caused by temporary brain (or retinal) ISCHEMIA WITHOUT tissue infarction; symptoms typically resolve within an hour and neuroimaging is normal. This patient's carotid bruit indicates atherosclerotic carotid disease that likely produced atheroembolism/low flow to the dominant hemisphere (arm weakness + aphasia). Because TIA markedly raises short-term STROKE risk, intensive SECONDARY PREVENTION is indicated: ANTIPLATELET therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel) to prevent thrombus, and a high-intensity STATIN (HMG-CoA REDUCTASE INHIBITOR, e.g., atorvastatin) to reduce atherosclerotic plaque and LDL, plus blood-pressure control, smoking cessation, and evaluation of the carotid stenosis (possible endarterectomy). THROMBOLYSIS (tPA) is reserved for ACUTE ischemic stroke with persistent, potentially disabling deficits within the treatment window; it is NOT indicated here because the deficit resolved and there is no infarct - giving it would only add hemorrhage risk. The other options treat unrelated conditions (MS, seizures, depression).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro/Pharm > TIA: transient focal deficit, no infarct, normal imaging; high stroke risk; secondary prevention = antiplatelet + statin + risk-factor control; tPA only for acute disabling stroke within window.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Deficit resolved + normal CT = TIA -> secondary prevention with a statin (and antiplatelet), not tPA.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on TIA vs stroke, thrombolysis (tPA) indications, statin/HMG-CoA reductase, or carotid bruit? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: tPA is for ACUTE ongoing disabling stroke, not a resolved TIA; MS/seizure/depression drugs treat other diseases.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: TIA -> antiplatelet + statin + BP/smoking control; tPA only for acute stroke with persistent deficit in window.

keywords.back: Transient focal deficit from ischemia, no infarction, normal imaging

keywords.front: Why not tPA in a TIA
keywords.back: Deficit resolved, no infarct - only bleeding risk
Acute disabling ischemic stroke within the thrombolysis window
Atherosclerotic carotid disease (embolic source; consider endarterectomy)
TIA = negative deficits; seizure = positive symptoms + postictal state

firstAid.detail: Neuro > tPA only for acute persistent stroke deficit.

memoryHook: A deficit that came and went with a clean CT is a TIA - a warning shot; you don't thrombolyse a warning, you prevent the next stroke with a statin (and aspirin).
